
---
title: "Cardiometabolic Risk Profiles and Obesity in Mexican Adults: An Exploratory Analysis of ENSANUT 2022"
author: "Amado Espinosa"
date: today
lang: en-US
abstract: |
  Excess body weight represents an important public health challenge in Mexico. According to ENSANUT Continua 2022, the estimated prevalence of overweight among Mexican adults aged 20 years and older was 38.3%, while the prevalence of obesity was 36.9%, based on measured body mass index (BMI). The study analyzed 8,563 participants. (Campos-Nonato et al., 2023). The World Health Organization (WHO) reports an age-standardized obesity prevalence of 36.1% among Mexican adults aged 18 years and older in 2022. This WHO estimate uses a different statistical presentation and population definition from the ENSANUT estimates; the figures should therefore not be interpreted as directly interchangeable. 
  Excess adiposity is associated with cardiovascular risk factors and chronic diseases, including hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. This study examines the association between joint anthropometric risk profiles and hypertension among Mexican adults using data from ENSANUT 2022. A survey-weighted cross-sectional analysis was conducted among 8,044 adults, adjusting for age, age squared, sex, and the adjustment category estrato. The primary model estimated a coefficient of 25.35 percentage points for adults with Obesity II/III and abdominal obesity, relative to adults with normal BMI and no abdominal obesity (95% CI: 19.45–31.26).

  This estimate represents a coefficient from a survey-weighted linear probability model, rather than a standardized population-average difference or a causal effect. Although the broader research motivation concerns cardiometabolic risk, the empirical outcome evaluated in this analysis was hypertension alone.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

if (!requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install the survey package: install.packages('survey')")
}

if (!requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Install knitr: install.packages('knitr')")
}

library(survey)
library(knitr)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 1. DATA
# --------------------------------------------------


# Run Quarto from the project root, or set ENSANUT_PROJECT_DIR
# to the directory containing the analytical CSV.
base_dir <- Sys.getenv("ENSANUT_PROJECT_DIR", unset = getwd())

input_file <- file.path(
  base_dir,
  "ENSANUT2022_cleaned_analytical.csv.gz"
)

if (!file.exists(input_file)) {
  stop(
    "Analytical CSV not found: ", input_file,
    ". Run Quarto from the project root or set ENSANUT_PROJECT_DIR."
  )
}

ensanut <- read.csv(
  gzfile(input_file),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA", "NaN")
)

required_vars <- c(
  "hypertension",
  "model_category",
  "edad",
  "sexo",
  "estrato",
  "upm",
  "est_sel",
  "ponde_f_anthro",
  "ponde_f_adult"
)

missing_vars <- setdiff(required_vars, names(ensanut))

if (length(missing_vars) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Missing variables: ",
    paste(missing_vars, collapse = ", ")
  )
}


# --------------------------------------------------
# 2. ANALYTICAL SAMPLE
# --------------------------------------------------

# Both candidate weights are required so that the
# primary and sensitivity models use the same adults.

complete_case <- complete.cases(
  ensanut[, required_vars]
)

model_data <- ensanut[
  complete_case,
  required_vars
]

cat("Original dataset:", nrow(ensanut), "\n")
cat("Complete-case analytical sample:", nrow(model_data), "\n")
cat(
  "Excluded observations:",
  nrow(ensanut) - nrow(model_data),
  "\n"
)


model_data$model_category <- factor(
  model_data$model_category
)

reference_category <- "Normal | No abdominal obesity"

if (!reference_category %in% levels(model_data$model_category)) {
  stop("Reference category not found.")
}

model_data$model_category <- relevel(
  model_data$model_category,
  ref = reference_category
)

model_data$sexo <- factor(model_data$sexo)
model_data$estrato <- factor(model_data$estrato)

# Ensure hypertension is numeric 0/1
model_data$hypertension <- as.numeric(
  as.character(model_data$hypertension)
)

if (!all(
  na.omit(unique(model_data$hypertension)) %in% c(0, 1)
)) {
  stop("hypertension must be coded 0/1.")
}

if (nrow(model_data) != 8044) {
  warning(
    "Expected 8,044 observations; found ",
    nrow(model_data),
    ". Check the analytical sample."
  )
}

# --------------------------------------------------
# 3. SURVEY DESIGN
# --------------------------------------------------

options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")

design_anthro <- svydesign(
  ids = ~upm,
  strata = ~est_sel,
  weights = ~ponde_f_anthro,
  data = model_data,
  nest = TRUE
)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 4. PRIMARY MODEL
# --------------------------------------------------

fit_primary <- svyglm(
  hypertension ~ model_category +
    edad + I(edad^2) + sexo + estrato,
  design = design_anthro,
  family = gaussian()
)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 5. ALTERNATIVE WEIGHT MODEL
# --------------------------------------------------

design_adult <- svydesign(
  ids = ~upm,
  strata = ~est_sel,
  weights = ~ponde_f_adult,
  data = model_data,
  nest = TRUE
)

fit_adult_weight <- svyglm(
  hypertension ~ model_category +
    edad + I(edad^2) + sexo + estrato,
  design = design_adult,
  family = gaussian()
)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 6. EXTRACT PRINCIPAL CONTRAST
# --------------------------------------------------

contrast_name <- paste0(
  "model_category",
  "Obesity II/III | Abdominal obesity"
)

primary_coef <- coef(summary(fit_primary))[
  contrast_name, ]

primary_ci <- confint(fit_primary)[
  contrast_name, ]

adult_coef <- coef(summary(fit_adult_weight))[
  contrast_name, ]

adult_ci <- confint(fit_adult_weight)[
  contrast_name, ]

primary_est <- primary_coef["Estimate"]
primary_se <- primary_coef["Std. Error"]

primary_low <- primary_ci[1]
primary_high <- primary_ci[2]

adult_est <- adult_coef["Estimate"]
adult_se <- adult_coef["Std. Error"]

adult_low <- adult_ci[1]
adult_high <- adult_ci[2]

survey_df <- degf(design_anthro)

# --------------------------------------------------
# ACHIEVED SAMPLE AND SURVEY DESIGN COUNTS
# --------------------------------------------------

n_adults <- nrow(model_data)

n_psus <- length(unique(
  interaction(
    model_data$est_sel,
    model_data$upm,
    drop = TRUE
  )
))

n_strata <- length(unique(model_data$est_sel))

cat("Achieved analytical sample:", n_adults, "\n")
cat("Distinct PSUs within strata:", n_psus, "\n")
cat("Sampling strata:", n_strata, "\n")
cat("Survey design degrees of freedom:", survey_df, "\n")

####check
#The achieved analytical sample contained
#`r format(n_adults, big.mark=",")` adults,
#distributed across `r n_psus` PSUs and
#`r n_strata` sampling strata.
#The survey design had `r survey_df` degrees of freedom.

# --------------------------------------------------
# 7. CHECK VERIFIED RESULTS
# --------------------------------------------------

cat("Analytical sample:", nrow(model_data), "\n")

cat(
  "Primary estimate:",
  round(100 * primary_est, 2),
  "percentage points\n"
)

cat(
  "Primary 95% CI:",
  round(100 * primary_low, 2),
  "to",
  round(100 * primary_high, 2),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Alternative weight estimate:",
  round(100 * adult_est, 2),
  "percentage points\n"
)
```

# Introduction

Hypertension is an important public-health concern, and excess adiposity is a relevant factor in its distribution. Body mass index (BMI) and abdominal obesity capture related but distinct aspects of adiposity.

International estimates underscore the magnitude of the challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the age-standardized prevalence of obesity among Mexican adults aged 18 years and older was 36.1% in 2022. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), using measured anthropometric data, reported that 70% or more of Mexico's population aged 15 years and older was overweight or obese in 2023 or the latest available year. These indicators describe different dimensions of excess body weight and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates. They nevertheless illustrate the substantial public-health burden associated with excess adiposity in Mexico.

This study examines the association between severe obesity (Obesity II/III) combined with abdominal obesity and hypertension among Mexican adults using ENSANUT 2022 data.

The principal comparison is between adults classified as Obesity II/III with abdominal obesity and adults with normal BMI without abdominal obesity.

The analysis is observational and cross-sectional. Its purpose is to estimate an adjusted prevalence difference, not to identify a causal effect.

# Data and design

## Data source and analytical sample

The analysis uses an analytical dataset derived from ENSANUT 2022.

The final analytical sample contains `r format(nrow(model_data), big.mark=",")` adults with complete information for the outcome, exposure, adjustment variables, survey-design variables, and both candidate survey weights.

The primary analysis uses the anthropometry-related survey weight (`ponde_f_anthro`). A sensitivity analysis uses the adult survey weight (`ponde_f_adult`).

Both models use the same observations and covariates.

## Survey design

The primary analysis uses the following survey-design variables:

- Primary sampling unit (PSU): `upm`
- Sampling stratum: `est_sel`
- Primary analysis weight: `ponde_f_anthro`

The primary model uses Taylor linearization for design-based variance estimation through the R `survey` package. The lonely-PSU adjustment is set to `"adjust"`.

The model also includes `estrato` as an adjustment covariate. This variable is distinct from `est_sel`, which identifies the sampling strata used in the survey design.

The achieved analytical sample comprised 8,044 adults in 432 distinct PSUs nested within 94 sampling strata. The survey design explicitly incorporates both the PSU clustering and the sampling-stratum structure. The variable `estrato` is included separately as an adjustment covariate; it is not the sampling-stratum identifier.

The achieved analytical sample contained `r format(n_adults, big.mark=",")` adults, distributed across `r n_psus` PSUs and `r n_strata` sampling strata. The survey design had `r survey_df` degrees of freedom.

## Outcome: hypertension

The analytical outcome is a binary indicator (`hypertension`).

The implemented definition combines reported prior diagnosis with measured blood pressure:

- A prior affirmative diagnosis is classified as hypertension.
- Among respondents without a prior diagnosis, hypertension is identified when mean systolic blood pressure is at least 140 mmHg or mean diastolic blood pressure is at least 90 mmHg.
- Respondents with valid mean readings below both thresholds are classified as not hypertensive.

Pregnancy-related diagnosis responses were kept separate from ordinary prior-diagnosis responses in the data-processing workflow.

**Protocol deviation:** the implemented outcome counts a prior affirmative diagnosis regardless of medication status. The initial plan described diagnosis in relation to treatment. This difference is disclosed as a deviation; no separate sensitivity analysis for this difference is reported.

## Exposure: BMI and abdominal obesity

BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by squared height in metres.

The workflow used age-specific anthropometric variables for adults aged 20–59 and adults aged 60 or older.

BMI categories were defined as:

| Category | BMI |
|---|---:|
| Underweight | <18.5 |
| Normal | 18.5–<25 |
| Overweight | 25–<30 |
| Obesity I | 30–<35 |
| Obesity II/III | ≥35 |

Abdominal obesity was defined using sex-specific waist-circumference thresholds:

- Men: ≥90 cm
- Women: ≥80 cm

The primary exposure variable (model_category) represents joint BMI and abdominal-obesity profiles. The principal comparison contrasts Obesity II/III with abdominal obesity against normal BMI without abdominal obesity. Other categories are retained as separate model categories where represented in the analytical data.

The reference category is normal BMI without abdominal obesity.

# Estimand and specification

## Primary outcome

The outcome analyzed in this report is hypertension alone, coded as a binary indicator (`hypertension`).

The composite outcome of hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia was part of the original research motivation but was not analyzed. It is not the outcome used to estimate the reported coefficient or apply the decision rule.

## Estimand

The analysis estimates a survey-weighted best linear projection (BLP) coefficient. It does not assume that the conditional expectation of hypertension is exactly linear in the explanatory variables.

Let Y denote the binary hypertension outcome. The explanatory variables include indicators for the joint BMI and abdominal-obesity categories, age, age squared, sex, and the categorical adjustment variable estrato.

The reference category is normal BMI without abdominal obesity.

The coefficient of interest is the coefficient on the category:

**Obesity II/III with abdominal obesity.**

It represents the coefficient on this category indicator in the survey-weighted linear projection, conditional on the other included regressors.

The fitted specification can be summarized as:

```text
Hypertension = intercept
             + joint BMI/abdominal-obesity category indicators
             + age + age squared
             + sex + estrato
             + projection residual
```

The coefficient is expressed in probability units. Multiplication by 100 expresses it in percentage points.

This coefficient is not a risk ratio, odds ratio, causal effect, or standardized population-average prevalence difference. It is a coefficient from the specified weighted linear projection.

## Decision rule

The substantive threshold established for the project is 15 percentage points.

The decision rule compares the complete 95% confidence interval for the coefficient of interest with this threshold:

- If the lower confidence limit is greater than 15 percentage points, the result meets the criterion for a substantively large positive contrast.
- If the upper confidence limit is below 15 percentage points, the result does not meet the criterion.
- If the interval includes 15 percentage points, the result is inconclusive relative to the threshold.

This decision rule is distinct from testing whether the coefficient equals zero.

For the hypertension outcome alone, the primary estimate is 25.35 percentage points (95% CI: 19.45–31.26), and the entire interval is above the 15-percentage-point threshold. Thus, the hypertension result meets the threshold. However, the original broader decision criterion concerned a cardiometabolic composite that was not analyzed; the full decision rule cannot be evaluated from this report.

# Description

The analytical sample includes `r format(nrow(model_data), big.mark=",")` adults.

```{r}


#| label: achieved-cell-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Achieved adult and PSU counts by sex, locality, and anthropometric profile"

# Identify each PSU within its sampling stratum
model_data$psu_id <- interaction(
  model_data$est_sel,
  model_data$upm,
  drop = TRUE
)

# Count adults in each analytical cell
adult_counts <- aggregate(
  rep(1L, nrow(model_data)),
  by = list(
    sexo = model_data$sexo,
    estrato = model_data$estrato,
    model_category = model_data$model_category
  ),
  FUN = sum
)

names(adult_counts)[4] <- "Adults"

# Count distinct PSUs within each analytical cell
cell_counts <- aggregate(
  psu_id ~ sexo + estrato + model_category,
  data = model_data,
  FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
)

names(cell_counts)[4] <- "PSUs"

# Combine adult and PSU counts
cell_counts <- merge(
  adult_counts,
  cell_counts,
  by = c("sexo", "estrato", "model_category")
)

knitr::kable(
  cell_counts,
  digits = 0,
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r")
)

```

The two groups defining the principal contrast contain:

- 1,122 adults in the Obesity II/III with abdominal obesity category.
- 977 adults in the normal BMI without abdominal obesity reference category.

These are unweighted sample counts.

# Results

## Primary estimate

The survey-weighted linear probability model estimates an adjusted prevalence difference of:

**`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * primary_est)` percentage points.**

The 95% confidence interval is:

**`r sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", 100 * primary_low, 100 * primary_high)` percentage points.**

The design-based standard error is `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * primary_se)` percentage points.

The model uses `r format(nrow(model_data), big.mark=",")` observations and `r survey_df` design degrees of freedom.

The verified project result is 25.35 percentage points (95% CI: 19.45–31.26).

The lower confidence limit is above the project's 15-percentage-point substantive decision threshold.

This comparison with the threshold is distinct from a conventional test of whether the coefficient equals zero.

## Sensitivity to survey-weight choice

```{r}
#| label: weight-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted prevalence difference under alternative survey weights"

sensitivity_table <- data.frame(
  Specification = c(
    "Primary: anthropometry weight",
    "Sensitivity: adult weight"
  ),
  Estimate_pp = 100 * c(primary_est, adult_est),
  SE_pp = 100 * c(primary_se, adult_se),
  CI_lower_pp = 100 * c(primary_low, adult_low),
  CI_upper_pp = 100 * c(primary_high, adult_high)
)

knitr::kable(
  sensitivity_table,
  digits = 2,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

The previously verified alternative-weight estimate is 25.59 percentage points (95% CI: 20.07–31.11), compared with 25.35 percentage points (95% CI: 19.45–31.26) under the primary anthropometry weight.

The point estimates differ by approximately 0.24 percentage points.

The substantive conclusion is similar under the two candidate weights.

## Exploratory analysis: Waist circumference as a continuous predictor of systolic blood pressure

An additional exploratory analysis examined the relationship between waist circumference and mean systolic blood pressure. This analysis was not specified in the original pre-analysis plan and was therefore treated as post hoc.

The analysis used the 8,044 observations included in the primary analytical sample. Twelve observations with missing mean systolic blood pressure were excluded, resulting in a secondary analytical sample of 8,032 adults. The primary sample and its complete-case definition were not modified for this secondary analysis.

Survey-weighted regression models were used to examine the association between waist circumference and systolic blood pressure, adjusting for age, age squared, and sex. The linear specification was compared with a natural cubic spline specification with three degrees of freedom to assess whether a strictly linear relationship adequately described the data. Variance estimation used Taylor linearization under the survey design.

Under the linear specification, each additional 10 cm of waist circumference was associated with an estimated 1.97 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure (95% CI: 1.53–2.40). The comparison between the linear model and the natural cubic spline specification provided evidence that the relationship was not adequately represented by a strictly linear function (working Rao–Scott test, p = 0.00092). The fitted spline suggested a positive association across much of the observed waist-circumference distribution, with flattening and greater uncertainty toward the upper tail. These patterns should be interpreted cautiously, particularly where observations are sparse and confidence intervals are wider.

| Exploratory result | Estimate |
|---|---:|
| Unadjusted association, per 10 cm | +3.17 mmHg |
| Adjusted association, per 10 cm | +1.97 mmHg |
| Adjusted 95% CI | 1.53–2.40 mmHg |
| Linear versus spline comparison | p = 0.00092 |
| Complete observations | 8,032 |


# Interpretation and limitations

The analysis estimates a positive adjusted association between the Obesity II/III with abdominal obesity profile and hypertension, relative to the normal BMI without abdominal obesity reference category. The estimated coefficient is 25.35 percentage points in the specified survey-weighted linear probability model.

The hypertension estimate exceeds the 15-percentage-point threshold, and the result is similar when the alternative adult survey weight is used. This conclusion applies to hypertension alone. Because the planned composite cardiometabolic outcome was not analyzed, the full project decision rule cannot be declared satisfied.

Several limitations qualify this finding.

First, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality.

Second, the estimate is conditional on the covariates included in the model and may be affected by residual confounding or measurement error.

Third, the primary estimate is a coefficient from a survey-weighted linear probability model. It should not be described as a causal effect or as a standardized marginal prevalence difference.

Fourth, the analysis is restricted to the available complete-case analytical sample and operational definitions.
The waist–SBP analysis is cross-sectional and cannot establish temporal direction or causality.

Besides that, the spline analysis indicates nonlinearity, but the exact shape at extreme waist measurements is uncertain.

The waist–SBP analysis used 8,032 complete observations drawn from the original hypertension analytical sample of 8,044. It should not be presented as an analysis of the entire ENSANUT adult sample.

Also, distinguish the observed SBP outcome from the binary hypertension definition. They are related, but not interchangeable.

The analysis identifies a substantial adjusted association between combined BMI and abdominal-obesity profiles and hypertension among Mexican adults. A complementary exploratory analysis treating waist circumference as a continuous measure also identifies a positive association with systolic blood pressure, persisting after adjustment for age and sex. The relationship is statistically nonlinear, although estimates at the extremes of waist circumference are less precise.

Together, these findings support the value of considering both general and abdominal adiposity when characterizing population-level cardiovascular risk. They also motivate further longitudinal research into individualized risk assessment, continuous health monitoring, and interventions supporting self-management of care. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

An independent Python reproduction using the same 8,044 observations, outcome, exposure categories, reference group, covariates, and anthropometry weight reproduced the primary point estimate (25.35 percentage points). The R and Python implementations therefore agree on the coefficient to the reported precision. Their variance-estimation procedures were not identical: the R analysis used Taylor linearization through the `survey` package, whereas the independent Python check used PSU-clustered standard errors. Standard errors and confidence intervals can consequently differ even when the point estimate agrees. The R survey-design results are reported as the primary inference.

# Methodological appendix {.unnumbered}

## A. Deviations from the initial analytical plan

The implemented hypertension outcome classifies a prior affirmative diagnosis as hypertension regardless of medication status. The initial plan described diagnosis in relation to treatment. This difference is disclosed as a protocol deviation. No separate sensitivity analysis was conducted for this difference.

The composite cardiometabolic outcome was part of the initial research motivation but was not evaluated in the reported analysis. Its complete-case sample size could not be established from the available analytical information. No estimate or inference is reported for this outcome.

The primary model uses `edad` as the age-adjustment variable and `sexo` as the sex variable.

## B. Survey-weight sensitivity analysis

The alternative adult-weight model estimates a 25.59-percentage-point adjusted coefficient (95% CI: 20.07–31.11), compared with 25.35 percentage points (95% CI: 19.45–31.26) under the primary anthropometry weight.

The two specifications use the same analytical observations, outcome, exposure, covariates, and survey-design structure. The alternative weight is therefore a sensitivity analysis of the weight choice, not an independent replication.

## C. Analytical implementation and reproducibility

The final report adopts the R implementation as the documented primary analytical workflow.

An earlier Python implementation produced a different estimate (19.03 percentage points). The discrepancy has not been fully reconciled. It is therefore treated as an unresolved difference between analytical implementations, not as a verified alternative result.

The R implementation and its corresponding analytical decisions are the definitive workflow for the results reported here. The discrepancy should be investigated before claiming that the two implementations reproduce the same analysis.


## D. Assessment of deviations from the revised pre-analysis plan
1. Reference protocol

The reference protocol for this assessment is the revised pre-analysis plan incorporating the instructor's feedback. It is the version used to assess which planned methods were retained, modified during implementation, or not completed.

This assessment distinguishes implementation decisions from analyses that could not be completed. Its purpose is to explain the implications of those differences for analytical validity, transparency, and interpretation.

2. Methodological assessment

The final analysis retained the central research question, the joint classification of BMI and abdominal obesity, the principal exposure contrast, and the survey-weighted linear probability model. The principal estimate was obtained using the anthropometry survey weight, with the adult survey weight used as a sensitivity analysis.

Several departures from the revised plan nevertheless require acknowledgment.

First, the operational definition of hypertension changed. The revised plan specified self-reported physician diagnosis with treatment, whereas the final analysis included self-reported diagnosis regardless of treatment, in addition to measured elevated blood pressure. This change may affect outcome classification and should be considered when interpreting the estimate.

Second, the planned cardiometabolic composite outcome was not evaluated. Its complete-case sample size and corresponding estimate cannot be established from the available information. No estimate is manufactured, and no conclusion is drawn about this composite outcome.

Third, the final adjustment set was narrower than originally proposed. The implemented model included age, age squared, sex, and `estrato`, while health-service affiliation was omitted. The planned interaction and subgroup analyses were also not completed. The variable `estrato` is an adjustment category associated with locality size; it is distinct from `est_sel`, the sampling-stratum identifier used in the survey design.

Fourth, although the plan proposed bootstrap-based variance estimation, the final report used Taylor linearization with the survey's stratification and PSU structure. This is an established design-based approach, but it is a departure from the originally specified procedure. Similarly, the planned logistic robustness analysis was not reported.

3. Interpretation and limitations

The principal model estimated an adjusted difference of approximately 25.35 percentage points in hypertension probability between the specified obesity profiles (95% CI: 19.45 to 31.26 percentage points). The corresponding sensitivity analysis using the adult survey weight produced a similar estimate of approximately 25.59 percentage points (95% CI: 20.07 to 31.11).

These estimates describe an adjusted association under the specified survey-weighted linear model. They should not be interpreted as causal effects or as proof that the exposure produces the observed difference. The confidence interval for the hypertension estimate lies above the prespecified 15-percentage-point threshold. This supports the threshold criterion for hypertension alone, but the full decision rule cannot be evaluated because the planned composite outcome was not tested.

The analysis is also limited by the complete-case sample of 8,044 observations. The implications of missing observations should be considered when assessing representativeness and potential selection bias. The independent Python reproduction agrees with the R point estimate; differences in variance estimation should be kept distinct from differences in the estimated coefficient.

4. Overall assessment

The final analysis provides a defensible, survey-adjusted estimate for the principal hypertension comparison. Its strongest features are the preservation of the central analytical question, the use of the complex survey design, and the sensitivity analysis with an alternative weight. Its limitations arise primarily from changes in outcome definition, a narrower adjustment strategy, and incomplete execution of planned secondary and robustness analyses.

The appropriate conclusion is therefore that the analysis offers evidence of a substantial adjusted association between the joint obesity profile and hypertension in the analyzed sample, while several prespecified questions remain unanswered.
